1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: The patient in this case was a 40-year-old male engineering management professional who presented to our hospital with the chief complaint of "recurrent cough and wheezing for 9 years, worsening for 2 years." Nine years earlier (2012), the patient developed cough symptoms after catching a chill during a business trip, with a small amount of white foamy sputum, throat pain, perceived difficulty speaking, and a softer voice, and accompanying staff could barely hear him speak. At that time, the patient also had wheezing after exertion and reported a marked decline in exercise tolerance. He was treated at a local hospital and improved after symptomatic "anti-infective and antiasthmatic" treatment. However, thereafter, the patient had similar episodes after each yearly "cold," occurring once or twice per year, all of which resolved spontaneously after symptomatic treatment and rest. In 2017, after another recurrence, he sought care at a hospital in Ningbo, Zhejiang, and was diagnosed with "asthma" by the local hospital. He was then treated with inhaled "budesonide/formoterol powder for inhalation 160 ug/4.5 μg." Despite regular inhalation, he still had intermittent cough and wheezing symptoms. In around Day 0, while on a business trip in Beijing, the patient again caught a chill and developed worsening cough and wheezing, and sought care at a tertiary hospital in Beijing. At that time, PFT suggested moderate obstructive ventilatory dysfunction, with a positive bronchodilator test (Figure 1). The CBC at that time was: WBC: 4.89^109/Lm, N:38.4%, EO:4.1%. Total IgE: 41.5 IU/ml. Allergens: inhaled dust mites, molds, cockroach, mugwort, dog hair, etc. were all negative. The patient was given intravenous "methylprednisolone sodium succinate" for 3 days, followed by oral "prednisolone acetate tablets" for half a month. The patient reported significant relief of cough and wheezing, after which treatment was changed to inhaled "budesonide/formoterol powder for inhalation 160 ug/4.5 μg" combined with "tiotropium bromide powder for inhalation," but the patient felt that cough and wheezing still recurred frequently thereafter. In approximately 17 months after Day 0, the patient visited a hospital in Shanghai, where PFT suggested moderate obstructive ventilatory dysfunction, with a suspiciously positive bronchodilator test (Figure 2). The chest CT plain scan report showed no obvious active lesions in either lung (Figure 3), and the patient was instructed to continue inhaled "budesonide/formoterol powder for inhalation 160 ug/4.5 μg" combined with "tiotropium bromide powder for inhalation." In October of the same year, the patient's cough and wheezing worsened again, and he was hospitalized at a hospital in Shanghai. During hospitalization, he was treated with intravenous infusion of "methylprednisolone sodium succinate" and nebulized "budesonide suspension for inhalation," after which his cough and wheezing symptoms were significantly relieved, and he was discharged. After discharge, he continued regular inhalation of "budesonide/formoterol powder for inhalation 160 ug/4.5 μg" combined with "tiotropium bromide powder for inhalation." Thereafter, the patient still had intermittent cough and wheezing. He then presented to Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University, for further diagnosis and treatment. Past medical history, personal history, and family history: unremarkable by self-report. Allergy history: history of penicillin allergy. Physical examination: T36.5℃, P 82 beats/min, R 18 breaths/min, BP 124/72 mmHg. Breath sounds were clear in both lungs, with expiratory wheezing audible. Heart rate was 82 beats/min, with regular rhythm. No obvious abnormalities were found on abdominal examination. No edema was present in either lower extremity. Ancillary examinations: CBC: WBC 10.92×109/L, N 64.7%, EO 0.2%, Hb 152 g/L, PLT 183×109/L. ESR: 6 mm/H. PCT: 0.05 ng/ml. IgE: 30 IU/ml. Autoantibodies tested were all negative: ANA, anti-dsDNA antibody, anti-nucleosome antibody, anticardiolipin antibody IgA, anticardiolipin antibody IgG, anticardiolipin antibody IgM, anti-RNP antibody, anti-Sm antibody, anti-SS-A antibody, anti-SS-B antibody, anti-SCL-70 antibody, anti-JO-1 antibody, anti-PM-Scl antibody, anticentromere antibody, anti-PCNA antibody, antihistone antibody, anti-ribosomal P protein antibody, anti-nucleosome antibody, anti-mitochondrial M2 sub-antibody, P-ANCA, C-ANCA, proteinase 3, and myeloperoxidase. Tumor marker CEA, urinalysis, stool routine, liver and kidney function, electrolytes, myocardial injury markers, etc. showed no abnormalities. ECG: sinus rhythm, normal ECG. Echocardiography: no abnormalities on echocardiography at rest. PFT suggested mild obstructive ventilatory dysfunction, with a negative bronchodilator test (Figure 4).

images.near_text: Figure 1: Pulmonary function testing at a Grade A tertiary hospital in Beijing showed moderate obstructive ventilatory defect, with a positive bronchodilator test.
Figure 2: Pulmonary function testing at a hospital in Shanghai: moderate obstructive ventilatory dysfunction; bronchodilator test suspiciously positive.
Figure 3: Non-contrast chest CT at a hospital in Shanghai; no obvious active lesions were seen in either lung.
Figure 4: Pulmonary function report from Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University: mild obstructive ventilatory dysfunction, bronchodilator test negative.

differential_diagnoses.name: bronchial asthma
supporting_evidence: The chief complaint was "recurrent cough and wheezing for 9 years, worsening over 2 years," with 1-2 episodes each year after a "common cold," showing features of recurrent episodic airway symptoms.
In 2017, he was diagnosed with "asthma" at a local hospital.
Pulmonary function testing in 2019 indicated "moderate obstructive ventilatory dysfunction, positive bronchodilator test (Figure 1)"
Pulmonary function testing in approximately 17 months after Day 0 indicated "moderate obstructive ventilatory dysfunction; bronchodilator test suspiciously positive (Figure 2)"
After repeated use of systemic glucocorticoids, "cough and wheezing were significantly relieved"
Expiratory wheezes were audible on physical examination.

The non-contrast chest CT report showed "no obvious active lesions in either lung (Figure 3)," which is consistent with the absence of obvious abnormalities on routine imaging in uncomplicated asthma.
opposing_evidence: Despite regular inhalation of budesonide/formoterol, intermittent cough and wheezing still occurred, and symptoms remained frequently recurrent even after adding tiotropium bromide.
Current PFT indicates mild obstructive ventilatory defect, bronchodilator test negative (Figure 4).
Total IgE 41.5 IU/ml; IgE this time 30 IU/ml; multiple items in the inhalant allergen panel were negative, not supporting a typical allergic asthma phenotype
Peripheral blood eosinophils not elevated: EO 4.1% in 2019, EO 0.2% this time

differential_diagnoses.name: Inducible laryngeal obstruction/vocal cord dysfunction (VCD/ILO)
supporting_evidence: At the time of the first episode, there was already "subjective difficulty speaking, a softer voice, and accompanying staff were almost unable to hear the patient's speech," suggesting possible functional abnormality at the laryngeal/glottic level.
The symptoms are mainly characterized by recurrent episodes, and chest CT imaging showed no obvious active pulmonary lesions.

Despite long-term regular inhaled therapy according to the asthma regimen, recurrent exacerbations still occurred, suggesting possible atypical asthma or asthma combined with upper airway dysfunction.
The PFT tracing shows an abnormal flow-volume loop appearance; upper airway obstructive lesions or glottic dysfunction should be suspected.
opposing_evidence: The physical examination documented "clear breath sounds in both lungs, with expiratory wheezing audible," more suggestive of lower airway obstruction.
A previous bronchodilator test was positive, and cough and wheezing were markedly relieved after systemic corticosteroid therapy; these findings cannot be fully explained by VCD/ILO alone.

differential_diagnoses.name: Central airway stenosis or fixed large airway obstruction (e.g., tracheal/main bronchial stenosis, endobronchial mass lesion, etc.)
supporting_evidence: The disease course is prolonged, obstructive ventilatory dysfunction persists, and the current bronchodilator test is negative, suggesting that in addition to reversible small airway disease, fixed airway obstruction should also be considered.
The flow-volume loop demonstrates an abnormal plateau-like pattern, raising concern for a large airway obstruction pattern.
Symptoms remained recurrent despite long-term inhaled ICS/LABA combined with LAMA, suggesting that asthma alone is insufficient to explain them
Chest CT shows essentially no obvious abnormality in the lung parenchyma; instead, it is necessary to consider that the symptoms originate from the central airways or upper airway.
opposing_evidence: The non-contrast chest CT report stated, "No obvious active lesions were seen in either lung (Figure 3)," and the provided CT images showed no clear evidence of an obvious central airway-occupying lesion or significant stenosis.

The symptoms previously improved significantly after anti-inflammatory, bronchodilator, and systemic corticosteroid therapy, which is not consistent with the typical pattern of persistent progression seen in most fixed organic stenoses.

differential_diagnoses.name: Tracheobronchomalacia/expiratory central airway collapse
supporting_evidence: Recurrent cough and wheezing, with essentially normal lung parenchymal imaging, but with long-standing symptoms, may be seen in dynamic central airway disorders.
An abnormal flow-volume loop may suggest dynamic central airway limitation
Routine static chest CT showed no obvious abnormalities and cannot exclude airway collapse occurring only during expiration or in a dynamic state
Poor control despite standard asthma treatment; structural or dynamic airway abnormalities should be considered
opposing_evidence: Phase 1 information did not provide evidence from dynamic inspiratory-expiratory CT, bronchoscopy, or typical positional/expiratory-related symptoms.
A previously positive bronchodilator test and effective corticosteroid therapy further support coexisting asthma or asthma as the primary consideration.

differential_diagnoses.name: Chronic obstructive airway disease/small airway disease (such as early-onset COPD or bronchiolitis obliterans)
supporting_evidence: Multiple PFTs all indicated obstructive ventilatory dysfunction, and the current bronchodilator test is negative, suggesting persistent airflow limitation
Long-term recurrent symptoms, with intermittent cough and wheezing persisting after inhaled therapy
No obvious active lesions were seen on chest CT; some small airway diseases may be atypical on routine non-contrast CT.
opposing_evidence: The patient is 40 years old. The stage 1 information did not provide a smoking history, dust/biomass fuel exposure history, or a clear occupational exposure history.
A prior positive bronchodilator test and marked improvement after systemic glucocorticoid therapy are more suggestive of asthmatic airway disease.
The provided CT images did not show definite emphysema or obvious typical signs of bronchiolitis.

differential_diagnoses.name: Non-asthmatic eosinophilic bronchitis
supporting_evidence: Chronic recurrent cough is a common manifestation.
Symptoms were markedly relieved after glucocorticoid therapy
opposing_evidence: The patient has definite wheezing and expiratory wheezes on physical examination, rather than a simple chronic cough phenotype.
Repeated PFT results indicate obstructive ventilatory dysfunction, whereas pulmonary function is usually not significantly obstructed in non-asthmatic eosinophilic bronchitis.
Peripheral blood eosinophils not elevated: EO 4.1% in 2019, EO 0.2% this time
IgE is not elevated, and multiple allergen tests are negative

recommended_exams.exam: Complete blood count + ESR + PCT + total IgE
Autoantibody profile (ANA, dsDNA, ANCA, anti-Sm, anti-SSA/SSB, anti-SCL-70, etc.)
Urinalysis + stool routine + liver and kidney function tests + electrolytes + myocardial injury markers
Repeat pulmonary function test + bronchodilator test

stage2_input.text: CBC: WBC 10.92×10⁹/L, N 64.7%, EO 0.2%, Hb 152 g/L, PLT 183×10⁹/L; ESR 6 mm/H; PCT 0.05 ng/ml; IgE 30 IU/ml. Autoantibody panel (ANA, dsDNA, ANCA, anti-Sm, anti-SSA/SSB, etc.) all negative; no abnormalities in tumor markers, urinalysis, stool routine, liver and kidney function, electrolytes, or myocardial injury markers. ECG: sinus rhythm, normal ECG. Echocardiogram: no abnormalities at rest. Outside-hospital PFT (2019-02): moderate obstructive ventilatory dysfunction, positive bronchodilator test. Outside-hospital PFT (2020-07): moderate obstructive ventilatory dysfunction, questionable positive bronchodilator test. Our hospital PFT: mild obstructive ventilatory dysfunction, negative bronchodilator test. Non-contrast chest CT: no obvious active lesions in either lung. Head and neck/chest 3D-CT: multiple calcifications of the trachea and bronchi, bilateral bronchial flattening, auricular and nasal cartilage collapse, collapse of the left thyroid cartilage. Further history: in 2009, redness, swelling, and pain of the right ear, diagnosed as auricular chondritis; recurrent after steroid treatment, with bilateral auricular collapse; in approximately 12 months after Day 0, nasal bridge collapse developed after a common cold.

differential_diagnoses.name: Refractory bronchial asthma
evidence: Presence of variable respiratory symptoms and signs, and objective test findings of variable airflow limitation
exclusion_reasons: Cough and wheezing caused by other diseases also need to be ruled out

differential_diagnoses.name: Heart disease
evidence: Common cardiac diseases that cause cough and wheezing include heart failure due to various causes, especially left ventricular dysfunction.
exclusion_reasons: The patient is a middle-aged man. Echocardiography showed no obvious abnormalities. At present, cough and wheezing caused by heart disease are unlikely.

differential_diagnoses.name: Upper airway disease
evidence: Including neoplastic lesions of the upper airway and glottic dysfunction, most commonly presenting predominantly with inspiratory wheezing; this patient previously had transient difficulty with phonation.
exclusion_reasons: Considering that the patient has not had any similar episodes since then, it is currently unlikely that upper airway disease is causing the patient's recurrent cough and wheezing.

differential_diagnoses.name: Various airway lesions, including space-occupying lesions and endobronchial tuberculosis, etc.
evidence: This type of disease usually presents with localized wheezing, and cough and wheezing symptoms generally persist.
exclusion_reasons: Chest CT frequently results in missed diagnoses. This patient has recurrent cough and wheezing triggered by repeated exposure to cold, which are not persistent and are inconsistent with this.

recommended_exams.exam: 3D CT of the head, neck, and chest
recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: 3D-CT of the head, neck, and chest showed multiple calcifications of the trachea and bronchi, bilateral bronchial flattening (Figure 5C), collapse of the auricles and nasal cartilage (Figure 5A, B), and collapse of the left thyroid cartilage.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has had recurrent cough and wheezing for as long as 9 years. Despite treatment with ICS/LABA and LAMA for asthma, exacerbations remained frequent, and PFT indicated persistent obstructive ventilatory dysfunction. The bronchodilator test results were inconsistent before and after testing, indicating that bronchial asthma alone cannot fully explain the condition. Prior non-contrast chest CT showed no obvious pulmonary parenchymal abnormality; therefore, further imaging evaluation of the upper airway, central airway, and systemic cartilaginous structures is needed. Head and neck-chest 3D-CT can directly assess whether the trachea, bronchi, larynx, and auricular/nasal cartilage have thickening, calcification, stenosis, collapse, or deformity, in order to address the key clinical question of whether the patient's cough and wheezing originate from central airway cartilage involvement rather than simple small airway disease. In addition, the patient had early symptoms of reduced voice volume and difficulty speaking; on further history-taking, there were also clues of auricular chondritis, bilateral auricular collapse, and nasal bridge collapse. This examination can unify the respiratory symptoms with ear, nose, and throat cartilage involvement, support the diagnosis of relapsing polychondritis, and help exclude simple vocal cord dysfunction, a fixed central airway mass, or other structural stenosis. For subsequent treatment, this examination can evaluate the extent and severity of airway involvement, determine whether there is potential airway risk, and provide a basis for systemic glucocorticoids, immunosuppressive therapy, and whether further airway interventional evaluation is needed.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Photographs of the patient’s left ear (Figure 5D), right ear (Figure 5E), and nose (Figure 5F) are provided.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Further inquiry into the medical history revealed a prior history of redness, swelling, and pain of the right ear, which was considered auricular chondritis. Although it improved after glucocorticoid therapy, it recurred repeatedly, followed by collapse of both auricles, suggesting that the auricular cartilage lesion was not incidental. A real photograph of the left ear was used for objective documentation of the morphologic change of the left auricle, directly showing whether there was auricular collapse, deformity, and other typical manifestations of cartilage involvement, thereby explaining the evidentiary chain that the patient, who had long been misdiagnosed as having refractory asthma, actually also had systemic cartilage disease. The question this examination was intended to address was: whether there were peripheral cartilage involvement findings that corroborated the central airway abnormalities, so as to increase confidence in the clinical diagnosis of relapsing polychondritis and reduce the possibility of misclassifying it as simple asthma, infection, or sequelae of local ear trauma. Ear imaging documentation can also be used to assess the extent of disease involvement, preserve baseline data, facilitate multidisciplinary consultation and comparison before and after subsequent treatment, and has supportive value for judging disease activity and supporting the initiation of immunosuppressive therapy.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Photographs of the patient’s left ear (Figure 5D), right ear (Figure 5E), and nose (Figure 5F) are provided.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The earliest and relatively clear clue of chondritis in the patient's history was redness, swelling, and pain of the right ear. The patient had previously been diagnosed with right auricular chondritis and responded to glucocorticoid therapy, followed by development of auricular collapse. Therefore, documentation of the right ear appearance has strong diagnostic relevance. A photograph of the right ear was used to directly confirm whether post-inflammatory cartilage destruction and collapse were present, and, together with the left ear, to determine whether there was bilateral auricular involvement, which is very important for relapsing polychondritis. The clinical question addressed by this examination was: in addition to the patient's long-term recurrent cough and wheezing, is there typical, visualized evidence of auricular cartilage involvement, helping to integrate the scattered respiratory and otorhinolaryngologic symptoms into the same systemic disease; it also helps exclude simple localized infection, traumatic deformity, or isolated ear disease. Because the patient subsequently required long-term immunosuppressive treatment such as glucocorticoids and methotrexate, retaining a baseline image of the right ear also helps with follow-up of treatment efficacy and assessment of disease progression.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Photographs of the patient’s left ear (Figure 5D), right ear (Figure 5E), and nose (Figure 5F) are provided.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: After a "common cold" in 2020, the patient gradually developed collapse of the nasal bridge, but this had not previously been taken seriously; together with bilateral auricular collapse and nasal cartilage collapse shown on 3D-CT, this finding suggests that, in addition to the airway, there is also nasal cartilage involvement. Clinical photographs of the nose can objectively document changes in the contour of the nasal bridge and directly demonstrate saddle-nose-like deformity or nasal cartilage collapse, thereby providing evidence of another typical site of involvement for relapsing polychondritis. The main question this examination is intended to address is whether the patient's chronic cough and wheezing are part of systemic chondritis, rather than isolated asthma or residual symptoms after a simple upper respiratory tract infection; at the same time, it strengthens the internal consistency of the external appearance evidence with central airway cartilage abnormalities and auricular cartilage lesions. This examination is valuable for both definitive diagnosis and differential diagnosis, can help exclude other causes such as simple congenital external deformity and traumatic nasal deformity, and provides a basis for MDT discussion, pretreatment baseline documentation, and subsequent follow-up comparison.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: In view of the patient's long history of recurrent cough and wheezing, we obtained a more detailed and supplemental medical history. The patient reported a history in 2009 of redness, swelling, and pain after pulling of the right ear. At that time, the patient also presented to a local otolaryngology hospital, where "right auricular chondritis" was considered, and improvement occurred after 1 week of oral "dexamethasone"; after self-discontinuation, the redness, swelling, and pain recurred. Later, the patient also presented to a specialty otolaryngology hospital, where reconstructive treatment was recommended, but the patient did not undergo further treatment. Thereafter, the patient noticed collapse of both auricles, and family members also noticed that the patient's external auditory canals were relatively small. Meanwhile, in approximately 12 months after Day 0, the patient reported that after a "common cold," rhinorrhea increased, and collapse of the nasal bridge gradually appeared, but the patient did not pay attention to this and did not receive further treatment. Relevant examinations were further completed. 3D-CT of the head and neck/chest showed multiple calcifications of the trachea and bronchi, flattening of the bilateral bronchi (Figure 5C), collapse of the auricular and nasal cartilages (Figure 5A, B), and collapse of the left thyroid cartilage. Clinical photographs of the patient's left ear (Figure 5D), right ear (Figure 5E), and nose (Figure 5F) are attached. The patient participated in a joint MDT consultation by the Department of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine and the Department of Rheumatology and Immunology.

Clinical photographs of the patient’s left ear (D), right ear (E), and nose (F).

8.final_diagnosis_and_diagnostic_basis.final_diagnosis: Relapsing polychondritis (bilateral bronchi, bilateral auricles, nasal cartilage, left thyroid cartilage)
diagnostic_basis: Multiple calcifications in the trachea and bronchi, with flattening of the bilateral bronchi
Collapse of the auricle, nasal cartilage collapse, and collapse of the left thyroid cartilage
In 2009, there was a history of redness, swelling, and pain of the right ear after pulling.
Bilateral auricular collapse; the family also noticed that the patient's external auditory canals were relatively narrow
Excessive nasal discharge, with gradual development of nasal bridge collapse
Joint MDT consultation by the Department of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine and the Department of Rheumatology and Immunology

treatment_plan: Prednisolone acetate tablets 40 mg orally once daily (taper by 5 mg every month)
At the same time, acid suppression, gastroprotection, and calcium supplementation were administered.
Prednisolone acetate tablets have currently been tapered to 20 mg orally once daily, and treatment is ongoing.
treatment_response: The patient reports no recurrence of cough or wheezing recently.
